title: Why the Sky Turns
objective: After this level you can explain that day and night, and the stars rising and setting, come from Earth spinning.
summary: Earth spins once a day from west to east, so the Sun and stars appear to rise in the east and set in the west.

cards.headline: The sky isn't turning. You are.
cards.body: Every sunrise looks like the Sun climbing up to meet you. It isn't going anywhere. Your patch of Earth is rolling toward it, and all night long the stars play the very same trick.

cards.headline: One spin, one day
cards.body: Earth spins on its axis, an imaginary line through the North and South Poles, about once every 24 hours. At any moment, the half facing the Sun has day and the half facing away has night. Nobody switches the Sun off at bedtime. Earth's spin simply carries your side of the planet from the sunny half into the dark one, and back again by breakfast.

cards.headline: Why everything rises in the east
cards.body: Earth spins from west to east, so your eastern horizon turns toward the Sun first. From where you stand, the Sun seems to climb up in the east and sink in the west. The Moon, the planets and the stars do exactly the same, for exactly the same reason. They aren't parading around us. Earth's spin sweeps them all across the sky the same way, like scenery sliding past a train window.

cards.fact: At the equator, Earth's surface moves at about 1,670 km/h.
cards.context: So why don't you feel it? Because you, the ground and the air all move together at a steady speed. Nothing rushes past you, so there's no wind in your hair and no coffee in your lap. The whole planet is one very smooth ride.

cards.headline: Daily spin: understood
learned: Earth spins once about every 24 hours
Day is the half of Earth facing the Sun
Earth spins from west to east
So the Sun, Moon and stars rise in the east

options.label: The Sun circling Earth
options.rationale: It looks that way, but it’s Earth that turns.

options.label: Earth orbiting the Sun
options.rationale: That takes a whole year, not a day.

options.label: The Moon blocking the Sun
options.rationale: That’s an eclipse, and it’s rare.

questions.explanation: Earth spins about once every 24 hours; the half facing the Sun has day and the other half has night.

questions.prompt: Why does the Sun rise in the east?

options.label: The Sun travels around Earth from east to west each day
options.rationale: Earth’s spin creates the Sun’s daily path, not an orbit of the Sun.

options.label: The eastern sky is closer to the Sun in the morning
options.rationale: Every horizon is the same distance from the Sun.

options.label: Earth spins eastward, turning the east toward the Sun first
Earth’s tilted axis points the east toward the Sun

questions.explanation: Earth rotates from west to east, so your eastern horizon swings into sunlight first and the Sun appears to rise there.

questions.prompt: From Level 1, stars are distant suns. Why do they rise in the east and set in the west, just like the Sun?

options.label: The stars all orbit Earth once every day
options.rationale: Stars are far beyond Earth; they don’t orbit us.

options.label: They are dragged along behind the Sun across the sky
options.rationale: Stars and the Sun each appear to move because of Earth’s spin.

options.label: The Moon’s gravity pulls the stars westward
options.rationale: The Moon doesn’t move the stars.

options.label: Earth’s spin sweeps them all across the sky the same way

questions.explanation: The stars aren’t moving across the sky. Earth’s west-to-east spin makes the Sun and every distant sun appear to rise in the east and set in the west.
